Restoration covers two jobs that have less to do with each other than the word suggests.

**Stopping a harm** ends something the ground was doing to somewhere else. Retire a field that was sending nitrate down its tile line and the nitrate stops; take a wet corner out of the rotation and the tillage stops with it. What gets claimed is a year that never happened, the one where the corn went in again, and the claim is capped by however much damage was already running. Ground that was not leaching cannot stop leaching.

**Starting a benefit** puts something on the ground that was not there before: native grass where there was bare fallow, roots deep enough to hold a hard rain where the crop was corn, shade the flock never had. Anyone can drive out in July and see whether it took, and the ceiling is whatever the site can grow. Permitting has ranked the work this way for decades: avoid and minimize harm first, then repair what is left. Restorative design ranks doing less harm a rung below putting something back [@reed2007].

The positions on the [farming axis](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions) from S1 to S5 each answer a question about harm. Is a farm still taking something off the ground, and is it the same use as before (S1) or a lesser one (S2)? Did the farm business survive losing the field (S3)? Was the ground already idle (S4)? Was it carrying a burden worth ending (S5)? **None of those five says anything about what the ground goes on to do.** A project can sit at S5, the strongest answer the axis has, and still run gravel and herbicide under the panels for thirty years, while an ordinary S3 conversion delivers all four [restorative functions](restorative-functions.qmd). Describing a project takes both readings. The one position outside that pattern is [S0](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions), which records a use that began rather than one that was lost, so it belongs with starting a benefit rather than stopping a harm.

The two jobs often want different ground, which water shows plainly (§-@sec-fn-hydrologic). To stop the nitrogen at its source the array goes on the field that was leaking, because the cropping stops with it. To catch what is already moving it goes on the flow path below, which may sit on somebody else's farm. Same objective, opposite pieces of ground.


## From Restorative Functions and Outcomes {#sec-deep-functions}

Two solar farms in the same county, the same size, the same panels, the same crop ground underneath. Under one, gravel and a herbicide schedule; under the other, a planting rooted deep enough to hold a summer storm where it falls.

Nothing about the land separates them. A project's size (§-@sec-transect) and what happened to the farming on it (§-@sec-farming-axis) set the outer limits of what is possible there. But what the ground ends up doing depends on how the design settled its competing pressures (§-@sec-pressures-ch), and above all on whether anyone was still pushing for restoration when the cheaper option was on the table.

So being [*restorative*](terminology.qmd#term-restorative) is not a property of a piece of ground. It is something a design produces, and on most sites it can be produced or held back. The **restorative functions** are the four things a design can aim at.

- **Water** (§-@sec-fn-hydrologic) — what soaks in, what runs off, and what the runoff carries with it
- **Ecology** (§-@sec-fn-biodiversity) — what can live there, and what can move through
- **Agriculture and soils** (§-@sec-fn-agricultural) — what farming gets from it, and what the ground underneath is made of
- **Community and economy** (§-@sec-fn-community) — what the people hosting it actually get


Read the figure by route, not by distance. Two things are missing from it. Carbon leaves by air, to everywhere and no one in particular, so the drawing has nowhere to put it. Land sparing is missing for a different reason: nothing travels at all, because its benefit is ground somewhere else that stayed as it was (§-@sec-benefit-range).

Microclimate is not on the list, though it used to be. The shade is real, and it is among the best-documented things an array does: daytime soil and plant temperatures fall, nights stay warmer, and the air under the panels is less drying (a lower vapor-pressure deficit) [@sturchio2023; @pinos2026; @barrongafford2019]. But shade is a mechanism, not an outcome, and its results are already counted elsewhere. Moisture held in the soil belongs to the water function. A cool refuge for what lives under the panels belongs to ecology. Relief for a shade-tolerant crop, shelter for stock, and shade for the people working there belong to agriculture. Listing microclimate separately counted the same shade twice. So the lexicon keeps [microclimate modification](terminology.qmd#term-microclimate) as a term for the mechanism and drops it as a function.

A function is not a position on the [farming axis](terminology.qmd#term-farming-axis). A project has one position, which records what happened to [agricultural production](terminology.qmd#term-agricultural-production) on its ground. It can deliver several functions at once, and the same function turns up at many positions. Pollinator habitat can be had under grazing (S1 or S2, depending on what the ground carried before), on ordinary converted ground (S3), and on spared or retired ground (S4 and S5) alike. Position only limits the functions where the ground is tilled every year, which rules out the ones that need an undisturbed [ground layer](terminology.qmd#term-ground-layer). Even then, that is a fact about tillage, not about the position, since S1 also covers pastures and orchards that are never plowed. Three ideas stay separate here. A [pressure](terminology.qmd#term-design-pressures) is a force pushing on the design, a [lever](terminology.qmd#term-design-levers) is something the design does about it, and a function is the result of the two. Treat the four functions as a palette rather than a scorecard, since no project delivers all of them and some work against each other.

A project needs two kinds of accounting. The [farming axis](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions) is mostly a record of [harm reduced](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-harm-benefit), since almost every position on it answers a question about what was lost. The functions are where benefits get promoted. The water function does both at once, and shows what the difference costs. **Avoided loading** needs the field that was leaking, while **interception** needs the ground below it, so a single goal can send a designer to opposite ends of the same farm. The two are checked differently, too. A benefit can be visited and looked at, while an avoided harm has to be argued against what would otherwise have happened. Neither ranks above the other, and on ground that was doing real damage, ending that damage is the bigger result.

**A note on "co-benefits."** The field usually calls these [co-benefits](terminology.qmd#term-cobenefit), and the word itself demotes them: a *co-*benefit is something that comes along with the real goal [@mayrhofer2016]. This lexicon names the functions as goals in their own right.

### Water

An array changes what happens to rain before it leaves, and what the water carries when it goes.

**Quantity** is the site's water balance. Panels catch rain and concentrate it along their drip lines while sheltering the ground beneath. Shade cuts evaporation and plant water use, so the soil generally stays moister, and the ground cover and grading decide how much water soaks in. At large scale, the bigger effect is on the water *budget* rather than the balance. Where solar replaces irrigated cropland, it ends that field's irrigation and eases the strain on an aquifer across a whole management area [@stid2022; @stid2025]. That only holds where groundwater rules keep the saved water from being pumped somewhere else [@zwickle2021].

**Quality** can be improved two ways, and they need opposite ground. **Avoided loading** stops the problem at its source, by putting the array on ground that was leaking nutrients, so the fertilizer and pesticide programs stop along with the cropping. On corn-ethanol acreage with documented nutrient losses, retiring that ground under unfertilized perennial cover would mean an estimated 54.8 million kg less nitrogen and 26.3 million kg less phosphorus applied each year [@sturchio2025croplands]. **Interception** deals with what is already moving, by setting perennial vegetation where runoff passes so it catches sediment, nutrients, and the pesticides carried on that sediment. That is the documented job of prairie strips in corn and soybean fields [@schulte2017]. Avoided loading needs the problem field itself, and competes with farming it. Interception needs the ground below that field, and works whether or not the field ever changes. Which one is available depends on placement, not management, so water is the function that [siting latitude](terminology.qmd#term-siting-latitude) buys the most of.

A creek below a twenty-acre array runs on water from several thousand acres, and twenty acres of changed cover does not show up in it. The same twenty acres draining one hollow does. That ratio is what the STRIPS work measured: a tenth of a field, planted where the water leaves it, held back more than 90% of the soil that used to go with it [@schulte2017]. So what a watershed notices is not the size of the array but how much of the ground draining past it the array sits on. A small project can matter more than a large one built somewhere the water is already diluted.

Size changes the shape of the flow as well. A few rows shed along their drip lines and the water leaves the way it always did, spread along the whole field edge. Put two thousand acres inside one fence and the same water arrives at a handful of culverts, in less time and in a smaller place. [Ramsey Renewable Station](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) absorbed the 100-year storm on sand at 3.4 megawatts. The same seed mix on tight soil, draining a bigger block to fewer outlets, is a harder storm to hold.

Water travels, so its benefits do. Moisture held in the soil stays **in place**. Slowed runoff and trapped sediment reach the field, the road, and the ditch just below before they reach anything farther away, which makes that the nearest and easiest form of this function to check. And irrigation that has been retired is felt across a whole basin. Direction decides all of it. Ground upslope of a problem can fix it, and identical ground downslope cannot.


### Ecology

Two halves: what can live on the ground, and what can reach it.

**Habitat** is built from the ground layer up. Flowering plants supply nectar and pollen, and the height and spread of the vegetation supply nesting sites, cover, and enough variety that many species can share one site. Panel shade shifts the timing, delaying bloom and producing more flowers late in the season [@graham2021], and the shelter underneath gives animals a cool place to wait out a heat wave. The seed mix sets the ceiling, but *timing* decides what actually happens. Mowing or grazing during nesting or bloom destroys the very resource the planting was meant to provide, which makes the maintenance calendar a design lever in its own right [@blaydes2022].

**[Connectivity](terminology.qmd#term-connectivity)** is the other half, and it is made or broken at four scales at once. Inside the array, the links are broken by things nobody thinks of as habitat design: access roads, gravel pads, mown strips, and a perimeter fence whose mesh decides which animals can get through. At the edge, what matters is whether the planting meets something already connected. A site that joins a fencerow or a streamside strip is part of a network, while the same seed mix fenced in the middle of row crops is an island. Across a landscape, many small arrays can act as stepping stones if they are close enough for animals to move between them, while a few large ones offer more interior and less edge. Which works better depends on the species, not on a general rule. Across a whole region, a fleet of arrays with compatible seed mixes and calendars is a network on paper. Whether it works as one in practice has not been measured (§-@sec-evidence-needs).

The corridor experiments are what make this more than an analogy. Patches of habitat linked by corridors exchange more individuals and gather more species over time than isolated patches of the same size. Butterflies were the study animal, because their movement can be watched directly (Haddad and colleagues, Savannah River Site corridor experiments; *trace before citing*). Two lessons carry over. Connectivity belongs to the arrangement, not to any one patch, so it cannot be claimed from a seed mix. And the distance that matters is set by the animal doing the moving. A bee foraging within 1.5 km, a butterfly crossing open ground, and a grassland bird holding a territory are three different design problems, so a connectivity claim means little until it names the animals it is for.

Both halves travel by way of living things. About 3,500 km² of US farmland lies within 1.5 km of existing and planned [utility-scale](terminology.qmd#term-utility-scale) solar, roughly a pollinator's foraging distance [@walston2018], and pollinators from solar sites have been recorded in neighboring soybean fields [@walston2024]. Farther out along the same route, the benefit shows up as a bird population rather than a single parcel [@walston2025].


### Agriculture and soils

The same ground does two things at once, and the same decisions govern both: what the farm gets out of the array, and what the soil under it is made of.

This function is not the farming axis under another name. The axis records whether farming continues on the ground the array occupies. This function asks what the array does *for* farming, and the two answers can differ. A project that has stopped all farming inside its own fence can still be the reason the field next door gets pollinated, and the reason the host farm is still in business.

Where the array sits in the landscape matters more for this function than for any other, because a planting can only reach the fields within a pollinator's range. And the order of bloom matters more than the amount, since a planting only helps a crop if it is flowering when that crop needs it.

Where permanent, lightly disturbed cover replaces tilled row crops, roots stay in the ground all year, traffic and tillage stop, and soil carbon and soil structure build back. That is the ordinary benefit of perennial cover, happening under and between the panels.

Construction cuts the other way, and it can cut deep. Grading strips off the shallow topsoil that holds most of the carbon. Trenching and heavy traffic compact what is left, and compacted ground holds back the roots that would rebuild it. So a site can begin its thirty years in debt rather than at zero. How big that debt is depends on how much earth had to be moved, which makes a [racking](terminology.qmd#term-racking) choice a soil decision made years before anybody picks a seed mix. A mounting system that can follow the slope leaves the ground roughly as it found it, and one that needs a flat surface means [mass grading](terminology.qmd#term-mass-grading). After that, how the cover is established, how it is grazed, and the [stocking density](terminology.qmd#term-stocking-density) carry the rebuilding. That rebuilding is slow and adds up over years, so it only happens if careful management keeps going the whole time.

The two halves reach people differently. Soil stays where it is, so that half is delivered **in place**, and whoever holds the ground keeps more of it than of anything else here. The service to farming travels. Pollination and pest control go out by way of living things to the fields within a pollinator's range, and the lease that keeps the farm running arrives by way of institutions. Carbon is the exception. It leaves by air, benefiting everyone and no one in particular, so it needs a market or a policy behind it before it is worth anything to the person holding the land.


### Community and economy

This is the one function that is not about the land. The others ask what the ground can provide. This one asks what the people hosting the project get. It is the result that the [community-acceptance pressure](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) and the [community-benefit lever](terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) both aim at, not another name for either. It covers three things: lasting local income and tax revenue, whether people can live alongside the array and had a real say in it, and whether the costs and the benefits land on the same people.

A project pays back in several forms at once: lease and royalty income, tax revenue and payments in lieu of taxes (PILOT), wages during construction and upkeep, savings for subscribers, and, where ownership is set up for it, an equity stake rather than just rent. The sums are not small. Landowners leasing cropland to solar earn three to four times what most crops return per acre [@sturchio2025croplands], and where farming continues alongside the array, the reported gains run higher still [@merheb2025]. The effects reach past the balance sheet. Federal biofuel policy has made conservation payments the less profitable choice across much of the same acreage, so solar income can make a conservation practice affordable when it was not before [@sturchio2025croplands]. Whether people can live with a project, and whether it treats them fairly, depends less on the size of the payment than on how the decisions were made. That is where benefit and acceptance come apart, and where a check without a fair process looks like a bribe.

::: {.how-to}
**Name the recipients separately.** "The community" is not one party, and a benefit to one can be a loss to another.

- **Landowner** — lease and royalty income; the party a land payment reaches first, and often the only one it reaches.
- **Tenant farmer** — frequently the party who *loses*. Nearly 40% of Central Valley agricultural land is rented, and the leading analysis of [agrisolar](terminology.qmd#term-agrisolar) economics there assumes returns reach landowning farmers, naming that as one of its own limitations [@stid2025]. This is the sharpest misalignment in the set, and the one a lease-income argument most often hides.
- **Neighboring residents** — bear [viewshed](terminology.qmd#term-viewshed), construction traffic, and glare, usually without a payment.
- **Local government** — PILOT and tax base, against service and road costs.
- **Tribal nations and communities of place** — treaty rights, cultural landscapes, and consultation standing that do not reduce to a payment.
- **Workers, subscribers, and ratepayers** — wages that may or may not be local, and savings that may accrue in another county entirely.

A project can score well on one of these and badly on the rest. Naming them is what keeps "community benefit" from collapsing into "somebody was paid."
:::

This function travels almost entirely by way of institutions: who owns what, who signed what, and which government collects what. That is why the list above does more work than any radius would. Part of it is genuinely local, since construction spending lands in the nearest town that can supply the work. But the money that matters most moves along channels drawn for reasons that have nothing to do with distance.


### Where benefits are delivered

A function is produced in one place and used in another. Ecosystem-service research treats that gap as its central spatial problem, since the area providing a service and the area benefiting from it have to be mapped separately [@syrbe2012]. Solar research has drawn the same line. @hernandez2019 sort a facility's outcomes into **sympatric** ones, which overlap the site, and **disjunct** ones, which land somewhere else, and give each a **serviceshed**, the area it serves.

What this lexicon adds is that the useful question is **not how far a benefit goes but which route it takes**. Nearly every function here reaches from the panel out to the region along some path, so sorting them by distance works badly. Sorting them by route works well, because the route decides who can check a claim and who receives the benefit.

**In place.** The ground that provides the benefit is the ground that receives it: soil carbon, soil moisture, forage and shelter under the panels. This is the easiest kind of benefit to measure, and the easiest to overclaim from, since it says nothing about anywhere else.

**Along a connection.** Everything that leaves the site leaves by some kind of network, and three networks carry almost all of it. **Water** carries runoff, sediment, nutrients, and recharge downslope, to the field just below and on to the ditch, the creek, and the aquifer. **Living things** carry pollination, pest control, and the spread of plants and animals, first within foraging range and then farther. **Institutions** carry lease payments, taxes, subscriptions, and easements, by way of ownership, contracts, and government boundaries. The first two follow the lay of the land and the third does not, but all three behave the same way in the one respect that matters: the benefit goes where the network goes, not where a circle drawn around the site would put it. A creek can carry sediment past a neighbor who gains nothing, and a lease can carry money to a county that never sees the array.

**By preservation.** [Land sparing](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions) delivers nothing that moves at all. Its benefit is ground somewhere else that stayed as it was, which makes it the one kind of delivery that has to be argued from what would otherwise have happened, rather than observed. It is still local, since a developer assembling acreage near a [substation](terminology.qmd#term-substation) chooses among parcels within a fairly small radius, so the ground a project spares is realistically in the same county. That gives the claim somewhere to be checked: against the local land market, and the sites that were genuinely in play.

One case runs backwards. Demonstration sites, field days, and school visits deliver value by bringing people *to* the array rather than sending anything out from it, which is much of what [Jack's Solar Garden](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-vegetable) produces. It is among the easiest things to design for and the most often left to chance.

::: {.how-to}
**What naming the route settles.** It answers three questions that are easy to mix up.

1. **Who can verify it.** In-place claims are measured on site. Connected claims need a gauge, a survey, or a document somewhere else, and preservation claims need the local land market and a credible account of what would otherwise have been built.
2. **Who captures it.** A landowner captures in-place benefit and can be paid for it. Benefits carried by water or living things go to people who have no contract with the project, so they need a policy, a market, or a watershed authority behind them to amount to more than goodwill.
3. **Which objection it answers.** A neighbor objecting to the view is describing something delivered at the fence line, and a developer answering with a carbon figure is describing something delivered everywhere and to no one. Both can be true, and neither is a reply to the other.
:::

### Evaluating outcomes

Each of the four functions has two outcomes, and together those eight are what a project can be judged on. Naming them separately matters because they move independently. An array can hold water on the site and still compact the soil under it, or pay a landowner well and give the neighbors nothing.

::: {.function-table}
| Function | Outcomes |
|:--|:--|
| **Water** | quantity, meaning what soaks in and what leaves · quality, meaning what the water carries with it |
| **Ecology** | diversity, meaning what can live there · connectivity, meaning what can move through |
| **Agriculture and soils** | food production, meaning what the ground still grows · soil quality, meaning what it is made of |
| **Community and economy** | financial security, meaning durable local income · livability, meaning whether people can live alongside it and had a real say |
: The eight outcomes, two to a function.
:::

Each outcome is measured on the same scale, from causing harm at one end to promoting benefit at the other, with a point in between where the project leaves that outcome no worse than it found it. @fig-outcomes-footprint plots all eight at once. **The middle ring is a zero point, not a pass mark.** It marks where harm turns into benefit. Nothing here says how far past it a project ought to go, and the lexicon leaves that question open on purpose.

The shape drawn there is a worked example, not a measurement. It belongs to a project that gives up food production for better soil and more ecological diversity, which is the trade a retired or heavily planted site makes. Reading a project this way does two things a single verdict cannot. It shows the trade-off, because a project that gains on one outcome and loses on another has a shape rather than a score. And it shows who is owed an explanation, because an outcome that falls inside the ring is a commitment the design did not keep.


## From Archetypal Forms {#sec-deep-archetypes}

Certain designs keep turning up. A farmer's flock under panels, a prairie strip in a wet draw, a retired irrigated field: the same few arrangements appear on ground that has nothing else in common. They recur because the [pressures](terminology.qmd#term-design-pressures) bearing on a project are never evenly matched. [Cost and financing](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) and [energy yield](design-pressures.qmd#sec-pressures) push hardest nearly everywhere, and where nothing pushes back the result is the same array anywhere in the country. Where something does push back, and keeps pushing through permitting and every round of cost cutting, the design settles into a shape that answers it. An [**archetype**](terminology.qmd#term-archetype) is one of those settled shapes. Nobody sets out to build one. The shape is what the pressures leave behind once they have finished arguing, and it is named after the fact, by people counting how often it turns up.

Scale and [farming axis position](terminology.qmd#term-farming-axis) decide which pressures can win. A farmer who owns the herd, the array, and the labor can put [agricultural production](terminology.qmd#term-agricultural-production) ahead of generation, because the array is sized to the milking parlor and no investor is waiting on a minimum return. At five hundred acres there is nobody left to make that argument, so restoration has to come from how the ground is run instead. This is also why an archetype can disappear. When the policy or the market that let a pressure win is taken away, the shape stops being built. Archetypes sort projects by how their pressures were settled, while [schemes that sort by hardware](terminology.qmd#term-overhead-interspace) sort them by what was built, and the two can be read side by side.

Where the site is changes which answers come cheap, because [a region weights the pressures differently](design-pressures.qmd#sec-regionality). In the irrigated West, groundwater law now meters and enforces the water shortage, so retiring fields above an overdrawn aquifer is the most ready-made restorative shape in the region. The same dry climate makes shade valuable enough to pay for the extra steel a crop canopy needs. Solar prairie strips deal with runoff from rain-fed Iowa cropland, so where rain is scarce and the water comes from a pump, that form all but disappears.

Six featured archetypes each come with a documented project, ordered from [farmstead](terminology.qmd#term-a1) to [complex](terminology.qmd#term-a5), and seven more are sketched briefly. The figure below arranges them differently, left to right by which lever did the restorative work, running from ownership through structure, management, and siting to contracts. That is the closest thing the six have to a natural order.


### Archetypes across scale and position

Every archetype below carries a short code under its name. It gives the archetype's [zone](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) on the scale transect, its [position](farming-axis.qmd#sec-positions) on the farming axis, and its [restoration mode](terminology.qmd#term-restoration-mode), meaning whether the restorative work is carried by the choice of ground, the array's geometry, how the site is run, who owns it, or what the contracts say. So `A1 scale · S1 farming · ownership-led restoration` describes a farmstead array on ground the farm's own animals keep using, made restorative by who owns it. The two tables sort the same forms by each of those in turn, with **featured archetypes in bold** and [the others](archetype-catalog.qmd#sec-further-types) in plain text. Arrays on buildings take no ground at all and sit at [A0](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones), off both tables.

::: {.zone-table}
| Zone | Forms that recur here |
|---|---|
| **A1 — Farmstead** | [**Barnyard Shelter Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-barnyard) |
| **A2 — Commercial** | [**Perennial Crop Canopy**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-permanent-crop) · [Vegetable Agrivoltaics](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-vegetable) · [**Marginal Land Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-marginal) · [Solar Fencerows](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-vertical-bifacial) · [Pivot-Corner Recharge](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-recharge) |
| **A3 — Community** | [**Perennial Crop Canopy**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-permanent-crop) · [**Solar Prairie Strips**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) · [Vegetable Agrivoltaics](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-vegetable) · [**Marginal Land Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-marginal) · [Pollinator Meadow Solar](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-community-solar) · [Solar Fencerows](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-vertical-bifacial) · [Pivot-Corner Recharge](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-recharge) · [Farm-Load Microgrid](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-microgrid) · [Brightfield](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-brightfield) |
| **A4 — Utility** | [**Perennial Crop Canopy**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-permanent-crop) · [**Regenerative Solar Grazing**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-grazing) · [**Retired-Irrigation Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-water) · [Restored-Grassland Solar](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-native-grassland) · [Solar Fencerows](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-vertical-bifacial) · [Farm-Load Microgrid](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-microgrid) · [Brightfield](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-brightfield) |
| **A5 — Complex** | [**Regenerative Solar Grazing**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-grazing) · [**Retired-Irrigation Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-water) · [Restored-Grassland Solar](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-native-grassland) · [Brightfield](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-brightfield) |
: Which forms recur at each zone. Bold entries are the six developed in full below; the rest are sketched. {#tbl-forms-by-zone}
:::

The crowding at A3 is the [feasible wedge](farming-axis.qmd#sec-wedge) showing up in practice. At that size, a project is big enough that management matters and small enough to site with care ([§-@sec-community-scale](restoration-modes.qmd#sec-community-scale)), so more forms are open there than anywhere else on the [transect](terminology.qmd#term-scale-transect). Every form listed has been built at that size, but climate, soil, water, market, and neighbors still decide whether it fits a particular site.

::: {.position-table}
| Position | Forms that sit here |
|---|---|
| **S0 — Created agriculture** | [Brightfield](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-brightfield) where the ground layer is grazed |
| **S1 — Primary agriculture** | [**Perennial Crop Canopy**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-permanent-crop) · [Vegetable Agrivoltaics](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-vegetable) · [Solar Fencerows](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-vertical-bifacial) · [**Barnyard Shelter Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-barnyard) · [**Regenerative Solar Grazing**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-grazing) on ground that was already pasture · [**Marginal Land Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-marginal) where stock stays on |
| **S2 — Secondary agriculture** | [**Regenerative Solar Grazing**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-grazing) on former cropland · [Pollinator Meadow Solar](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-community-solar) where hives are kept |
| **S3 — Ordinary-land siting** | [Pollinator Meadow Solar](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-community-solar) · [Restored-Grassland Solar](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-native-grassland) · [Farm-Load Microgrid](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-microgrid) |
| **S4 — Low-productivity siting** | [**Marginal Land Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-marginal) · [Pivot-Corner Recharge](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-recharge) · [Brightfield](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-brightfield) · [Farm-Load Microgrid](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-microgrid) |
| **S5 — Impaired-land siting** | [**Solar Prairie Strips**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-prairie-strips) · [**Retired-Irrigation Solar**](archetype-catalog.qmd#arch-water) |
: The same forms arranged by what happened to agricultural production, rather than by size. A form appearing at more than one position is one whose ground layer can be run more than one way, or one whose position turns on what the ground carried before it. {#tbl-forms-by-position}
:::

The sharing side of the table is wider than it looks, for two different reasons. Keeping a *crop* under panels takes geometry that costs money, which is why only three forms manage it. Keeping a *pasture* takes nothing but the decision to put the array where the stock already were, which is why grazing reaches the largest sizes without leaving the sharing side at all. On the sparing side, siting does the work. Grazing is the one form that reaches utility scale without giving up a productive ground layer, and that is most of why it is the most common [restorative](terminology.qmd#term-restorative) practice on large arrays.
